engine.summary: Create and start a new container from an image
engine.description: Combines create and start. Pulls the image if it is not present locally, creates a writable layer, configures namespaces and cgroups, and starts the container process. The container stops when its main process exits.

examples.title: Detached web server
examples.explain: HOST:CONTAINER maps port 8080 on loopback to 80 in the container.

examples.title: One-off command
examples.explain: --rm removes the container when it exits.

examples.title: Interactive shell
examples.explain: -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a TTY.

advanced.title: Hardened service
advanced.command: docker run -d --name api --user 10001:10001 --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --security-opt no-new-privileges --memory 256m --pids-limit 128 acme/api:1.4

engine.output: The container ID is printed on success. Use docker ps to see state and docker logs for output.
mistakes: Using shell form in CMD/ENTRYPOINT hides signals and can leave the container running after the app crashes.
Publishing a port on 0.0.0.0 when the service should be local-only. Use 127.0.0.1:HOST:CONTAINER.
Forgetting that a container exits as soon as its main process exits; daemonizing the app stops the container.
security: Avoid --privileged. Drop capabilities and run as a non-root user.
Never mount /var/run/docker.sock into an application container.

engine.summary: Create a container without starting it
engine.description: Allocates the container, writable layer, network configuration and name, but does not start the process. Useful for preparing a container that will be started later or by an external system.

examples.title: Prepare a worker
examples.command: docker create --name worker -e MODE=batch alpine sleep 3600

engine.output: Prints the container ID. The container is in the created state.
mistakes: Expecting the container to run; use docker start or docker run.
Assuming create validates the command exists inside the image.

engine.summary: Start one or more stopped containers
engine.description: Starts an existing container, reusing its configuration and writable layer. Use -a to attach and -i to keep stdin open.
engine.output: Prints the container name or ID when started.
mistakes: Start does not create a new container; use run for that.
Attaching to a service with -a can let Ctrl-C terminate it.

engine.summary: Stop one or more running containers gracefully
engine.description: Sends SIGTERM, waits for the timeout (10 seconds by default), then sends SIGKILL. The container remains in the exited state until removed.
engine.output: The container name or ID is printed after it stops.
mistakes: Assuming stop removes the container; it does not.
Using a grace period shorter than the application shutdown time.
security: Handle SIGTERM in the application to finish in-flight requests and close connections.

engine.description: Stop and then start a container. The writable layer and configuration are preserved.
mistakes: Using restart to apply a new image or environment; recreate the container instead.

engine.summary: Run a command in a running container
engine.description: Starts an additional process inside an existing container’s namespaces. It does not restart or replace the main process. Use -it for an interactive shell.

examples.title: One-off inspection
examples.output: nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test is successful

engine.output: Streams the command output. The exit code comes from the executed command.
mistakes: Using exec when the container is stopped; it requires a running container.
Installing debugging tools into production images instead of using an ephemeral debug container.

engine.summary: Fetch the logs of a container
engine.description: Reads the container’s stdout/stderr through the configured logging driver. Streaming and tailing are supported. Only local drivers keep logs accessible to this command.
engine.output: The application output, optionally timestamped.
mistakes: Expecting logs when the app writes to a file inside the container.
Forgetting that remote logging drivers may make docker logs empty.

engine.description: Lists running containers by default. Use -a for all states, -s for sizes, and --filter for labels, names, status and health.
engine.output: CONTAINER ID   IMAGE   COMMAND   CREATED   STATUS   PORTS   NAMES
mistakes: Forgetting -a and concluding a stopped container was deleted.
Parsing the default table in scripts instead of using --format json.

engine.summary: Return low-level information about Docker objects
engine.description: Returns JSON describing a container, image, volume, network or other object. Use --format with Go templates to extract fields. This is the primary diagnostic command.
engine.output: A JSON array, even for a single object.
mistakes: Forgetting that the output is an array; use index 0 or --format.
Reading env values that may contain secrets in logs or screenshots.

engine.description: Deletes stopped containers and their writable layers. Use -f to stop and remove a running container, and -v to remove anonymous volumes associated with it.
engine.output: The removed container name or ID.
mistakes: Using rm -f in automation where graceful stop matters.
Assuming named volumes are removed with the container; they are not unless -v or volume prune.
security: Removal is irreversible. Confirm the container name and that data is in a volume or external store.

engine.summary: Copy files between a container and the host
engine.description: Copies files or directories in either direction. The container may be running or stopped. Paths inside the container are resolved relative to its root filesystem.
engine.syntax: docker cp [OPTIONS] CONTAINER:SRC_PATH DEST_PATH | SRC_PATH CONTAINER:DEST_PATH
mistakes: Using cp for live database data; use a native dump or volume backup.
Forgetting ownership: copied files retain UID/GID metadata where supported.

engine.summary: Display a live stream of container resource usage
engine.description: Shows CPU, memory, network, block I/O and PID counts. Use --no-stream for a single sample. CPU percent is relative to one core on most platforms.
engine.output: NAME  CPU %  MEM USAGE / LIMIT  MEM %  NET I/O  BLOCK I/O  PIDS
mistakes: Treating a single snapshot as a baseline.
Reading cumulative network/block counters as rates without taking deltas.

engine.summary: Pause all processes in a container
engine.description: Uses the freezer cgroup to suspend processes. The container keeps its state and can be resumed with unpause.
mistakes: Pausing a production service without draining traffic first.

engine.description: Resumes a container previously paused with docker pause.

engine.summary: List port mappings for a container
engine.description: Prints the host binding(s) for a container port or all published ports.
mistakes: Confusing EXPOSE with published ports; port shows only actual bindings.

engine.summary: Update resource limits of a container
engine.description: Changes CPU, memory, restart policy and related host configuration on an existing container. Some changes require a restart to take effect.
mistakes: Lowering a limit below current usage can trigger OOM kills.
Assuming every option applies live.

engine.summary: Create an image from a container’s changes
engine.description: Creates a new image from the container’s writable layer. Useful for debugging or one-off snapshots, not for reproducible production builds.
mistakes: Using commit as a build process; changes are not reproducible and history is opaque.
Committing secrets or temporary files from the container filesystem.
security: A committed image can contain secrets, SSH keys and temporary files. Prefer a Dockerfile.

engine.summary: Build an image from a Dockerfile
engine.description: Builds an image from a Dockerfile and build context using BuildKit by default. Supports target stages, build args, secrets, cache import/export and multi-platform output through buildx.
engine.output: BuildKit step output; the final image ID on success.
mistakes: Copying the whole context before dependency installation, destroying cache hits.
Passing secrets in --build-arg; they persist in image history.
Building from a large context without a .dockerignore.
security: Use --secret for credentials, not ARG/ENV.
Scan the result and pin base images for production.

engine.description: The buildx entry point supports multi-platform builds, cache import/export, attestations, and alternate builders. Requires a builder with the appropriate driver for multi-platform output.
engine.output: Build progress; multi-platform images must be pushed or exported, not loaded.
mistakes: Using --load with multiple platforms; an image index cannot be loaded into the local store.
Forgetting --push for registry output.

engine.summary: Pull an image from a registry
engine.description: Downloads the manifest and missing layers for a reference. Supports --platform and digest references.
engine.output: Pull progress with layer status; "Status: Downloaded newer image" or "Image is up to date".
mistakes: Using latest in production; the tag moves.
Pulling a tag and assuming the digest will not change.
security: Verify signatures/provenance for sensitive environments; pin digests for reproducibility.

engine.summary: Push an image to a registry
engine.description: Uploads image layers and the manifest to the registry encoded in the reference. The image must be tagged with the full registry path.
engine.output: Layer upload progress and the resulting digest.
mistakes: Pushing a local name without a registry path; it targets Docker Hub.
Assuming docker tag uploads the image.
security: Authenticate with a scoped token via --password-stdin or a credential helper.

engine.summary: List images in the local store
engine.description: Lists repositories, tags, image IDs, creation time and size. Use --digests for digests, --filter dangling=true for untagged images.
engine.output: REPOSITORY  TAG  IMAGE ID  CREATED  SIZE
mistakes: Confusing shared size with unique size when planning disk cleanup.
Assuming an image is unused because no container currently runs from it.

engine.summary: Create a tag for a source image
engine.description: Creates another local name for an existing image. It does not copy layers or upload anything. The target reference can include a registry host.
mistakes: Expecting tag to push or duplicate the image.
Tagging a local image with a registry path you cannot authenticate to.

engine.description: Removes an image reference and its layers when not used by other images. Fails if a container (running or stopped) references the image unless forced.
mistakes: Forcing removal of an image used by a running container.
Assuming a tag removal deletes every layer if another tag shares it.
security: Removal is irreversible without re-pulling or a saved archive.

engine.summary: Show the history of an image
engine.description: Lists layers and the instructions that created them, with sizes and IDs. Use it to find large layers, accidental secrets and unexpected commands.
engine.output: IMAGE  CREATED  CREATED BY  SIZE  COMMENT
mistakes: Assuming every layer is a Dockerfile instruction; metadata and imported history differ.
security: History can reveal credentials passed in ARG. Never use ARG for secrets.

engine.summary: Save image(s) to a tar archive
engine.description: Exports image layers and metadata to a tar file for offline transfer. Load restores it with docker load.
mistakes: Using save/load as a registry replacement for large numbers of images; it does not deduplicate across archives.

engine.summary: Load images from a tar archive
engine.description: Imports images created by docker save. Preserves tags and digests where present.
engine.output: Loaded image: acme/api:1.4

engine.description: Creates a named volume managed by Docker. Volumes persist independently of containers and are the recommended storage for application state.

examples.title: With driver
examples.command: docker volume create --driver local --opt type=tmpfs app-tmp

mistakes: Assuming a volume is bound to one container; multiple containers can mount it.
Using an anonymous volume when you need a stable name.

engine.description: Lists named volumes with driver and scope. Anonymous volumes have long hashes and are harder to manage.
Returns the mountpoint, driver, labels, options and scope. The mountpoint is on the Docker host, not inside the container.
mistakes: Editing the mountpoint directly while containers are using it; use a container or backup workflow.

engine.description: Deletes volumes that are not in use by a container. Use -f to force removal, which can orphan running containers.
mistakes: Forcing removal of a volume attached to a running database.
Assuming down removes volumes; use down -v deliberately.
security: Irreversible data loss. Back up and verify first.

engine.description: Removes volumes not used by any container. With --all it removes all unused volumes, including named ones.
mistakes: Running it on a host with stopped-but-needed data volumes.
Assuming a detached volume is unused; verify with df -v.
security: Destructive. Back up and confirm scope.

engine.description: Creates a user-defined network. Bridge is the default driver and provides embedded DNS on the network. Options include subnet, gateway and internal.
mistakes: Using the default bridge and expecting name resolution; create a user-defined network.
Overlapping subnets with the host or VPN.

engine.description: Lists built-in and user-defined networks with driver, scope and labels.
Returns subnet, gateway, connected containers and their IPs, and options. The fastest way to verify membership and addressing.

engine.summary: Connect a container to a network
engine.description: Attaches a running container to one or more networks. Supports --alias and static IP options.

examples.title: Alias
examples.command: docker network connect --alias database backend-net api

mistakes: Assuming the container can resolve names on the new network without checking DNS.

engine.description: Removes user-defined networks. Fails if containers are still attached.
mistakes: Trying to remove the default bridge/host/none networks.

engine.description: Removes user-defined networks not used by any container.
security: Verify no external containers depend on the network.

engine.description: Reports engine version, storage driver, cgroup driver, kernel, CPU/memory, container counts, plugins, security options and warnings.
engine.output: Server: Docker Engine ... Storage Driver: overlayfs ...
mistakes: Ignoring the Warnings section; it often explains degraded behaviour.

engine.summary: Show Docker client and server versions
engine.description: Prints client and server version, API version, Go version, OS/arch and build details. A missing Server section means the client cannot reach the daemon.
engine.output: Client: ... Version: 29.x ... Server: ... Version: 29.x
mistakes: Assuming a client-only output is a complete installation.

engine.description: Streams daemon events for containers, images, networks, volumes and more. Filter by type, event, label, container or image. The daemon keeps only recent events.
mistakes: Expecting long-term history; ship events to a log pipeline for retention.
Forgetting that --until now is evaluated when the command starts.

engine.description: Summarizes size and reclaimable space for images, containers, volumes and build cache. Use -v for per-object detail.
engine.output: TYPE  TOTAL  ACTIVE  SIZE  RECLAIMABLE
mistakes: Equating shared image size with unique disk usage.

engine.description: Removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and build cache. With -a it removes all unused images; with --volumes it also removes unused volumes.
mistakes: Running -a --volumes on a host with data you have not backed up.
Using prune to fix a problem without understanding what is consuming space.
security: Destructive and irreversible. Read the confirmation and back up volumes.

engine.description: Stores credentials for a registry. Use --password-stdin to avoid putting the secret in argv or shell history. Credentials go to a helper or config.json.
mistakes: Passing the password as an argument.
Committing ~/.docker/config.json to a repository.
security: Authenticating to a malicious registry can leak credentials; verify the host.

engine.description: Removes stored credentials for a registry host.
Searches Docker Hub by term and returns name, description, stars and official status. It does not search arbitrary registries.
mistakes: Assuming search covers private registries or enterprise catalogs.
Pulling an unofficial image without reviewing its source and maintenance.
security: Prefer official or verified publishers; scan images before use.

engine.description: Create, inspect, use and remove named daemon endpoints, including SSH and TLS. Contexts keep remote engines one command away.
mistakes: Running destructive commands against the wrong context.
Exposing a remote daemon over unauthenticated TCP instead of SSH/TLS.
security: Treat a production context as privileged access. Verify the active context before pruning.

engine.description: Removes BuildKit cache. Use --keep-storage to retain a ceiling, or --all to remove all cache including in-use records.
mistakes: Pruning during an active build.
Assuming build cache is part of the image size; it is separate.

compose.description: Builds or pulls images as needed, creates networks/volumes, and starts services in dependency order. -d runs detached; --wait waits for healthy/running state.
compose.output: Network and container creation logs; with -d the command returns after start (or health with --wait).
mistakes: Assuming depends_on waits for readiness; add health conditions.
Forgetting that down -v deletes volumes.

compose.description: Stops services and removes containers and the default network. Volumes are kept unless --volumes is passed. --remove-orphans removes services no longer in the file.
mistakes: Using -v casually; it destroys named volume data.
Expecting down to remove externally created networks/volumes.
security: Back up volumes before using -v.

compose.description: Shows containers for the current project with state, health and ports. --all includes stopped one-shot services.
mistakes: Confusing container state with application readiness; check health and logs.

compose.description: Aggregates logs from project services. -f follows, --tail limits, and service names filter output.
mistakes: Using logs to debug a container that writes to files instead of stdout.

compose.summary: Resolve and validate the Compose model
compose.description: Resolves variables, merges multiple files, validates the schema and prints the canonical model. --quiet only reports errors. Essential in CI.
mistakes: Skipping validation and discovering interpolation errors at deploy time.
Assuming config starts containers; it does not.

compose.description: Builds images for services with a build section. Supports --no-cache, --pull and service selection.
Pulls the image for each service that has an image (not only build). Use --ignore-buildable to skip build-backed services.

compose.summary: Run a command in a running service
compose.description: Like docker exec but resolves the service name and uses the service container. -T disables TTY allocation for scripts.

examples.title: Non-interactive
examples.command: docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U app app > backup.sql

mistakes: Using exec for a one-off service that is not running; use run instead.
Forgetting -T in CI pipelines.

compose.summary: Run a one-off command in a service
compose.description: Creates a new container for a service and runs a command. --rm removes it afterwards. Unlike exec, it can start a stopped service container.

examples.title: One-off task
examples.command: docker compose run --rm api npm run migrate

mistakes: Using run for long-lived services; it creates a new container outside the normal service lifecycle.
Forgetting --rm and accumulating one-off containers.

compose.description: Restarts service containers without recreating them. Configuration or image changes are not applied; use up -d --force-recreate for that.
mistakes: Expecting a new image or env change to take effect; recreate instead.

compose.description: Stops running service containers without removing them.
Starts previously created service containers. Does not recreate or apply config changes.
Removes stopped containers for services. -f skips confirmation; -v removes anonymous volumes.
Sets the number of containers for a service on a single host. Ports must not collide; use a proxy or omit fixed host ports.
mistakes: Scaling a service with a fixed published port; only one container can bind it.
Expecting load balancing; Compose has no built-in service VIP.

compose.summary: Watch and sync service source changes
compose.description: Watches the build context and rebuilds or syncs files for services with a develop.watch configuration.
Streams events for the project’s containers with Compose context.
Shows the image, tag, image ID and size for each service container.
Lists volumes used by the project and whether they are external.
Lists projects with status and config file paths. --all includes stopped projects.
Pushes images for services with an image field.
Creates containers for services without starting them.
Sends SIGKILL to service containers. Use only when graceful stop is not possible.
security: SIGKILL prevents cleanup and can corrupt state; prefer stop.

dockerfile.name: FROM
dockerfile.summary: Sets the base image for a build stage. Every Dockerfile starts with FROM (or ARG before FROM).
dockerfile.description: Sets the base image for a build stage. Every Dockerfile starts with FROM (or ARG before FROM). This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Pin a version for reproducible builds; use digests in regulated environments.
security: Prefer minimal base images to reduce attack surface.

dockerfile.name: RUN
dockerfile.summary: Executes a command during the build in a new layer. Use exec form or shell form; combine related commands to reduce layers.
dockerfile.description: Executes a command during the build in a new layer. Use exec form or shell form; combine related commands to reduce layers. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Never put secrets in RUN arguments; use --mount=type=secret.
security: Clean package caches in the same RUN to avoid bloating the layer.

dockerfile.name: CMD
dockerfile.summary: Provides the default command or arguments for the container. Overridden by arguments to docker run. Only the last CMD takes effect.
dockerfile.description: Provides the default command or arguments for the container. Overridden by arguments to docker run. Only the last CMD takes effect. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Use exec form for correct signal handling.
security: Do not use CMD for build steps.

dockerfile.name: ENTRYPOINT
dockerfile.summary: Sets the executable that runs when the container starts. Runtime arguments are appended to ENTRYPOINT (or replace CMD).
dockerfile.description: Sets the executable that runs when the container starts. Runtime arguments are appended to ENTRYPOINT (or replace CMD). This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Shell form wraps the command in /bin/sh and can break signals.
security: Use an entrypoint script ending in exec "$@" if you need setup.

dockerfile.name: COPY
dockerfile.summary: Copies files from the build context or a previous stage into the image.
dockerfile.description: Copies files from the build context or a previous stage into the image. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Copy dependency manifests before source for better caching.
security: Use --chown instead of a later chown layer.

dockerfile.name: ADD
dockerfile.summary: Like COPY but also supports URLs and automatic tar extraction. Prefer COPY unless you need those behaviours.
dockerfile.description: Like COPY but also supports URLs and automatic tar extraction. Prefer COPY unless you need those behaviours. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: ADD from a URL does not use the build cache the way COPY does.
security: Automatic extraction can be surprising; be explicit.

dockerfile.name: WORKDIR
dockerfile.summary: Sets the working directory for subsequent instructions and the runtime. Creates the directory if needed.
dockerfile.description: Sets the working directory for subsequent instructions and the runtime. Creates the directory if needed. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Use absolute paths to avoid confusion.
security: WORKDIR does not create a layer.

dockerfile.name: ENV
dockerfile.summary: Sets environment variables for the build and the runtime container. Values persist in image metadata.
dockerfile.description: Sets environment variables for the build and the runtime container. Values persist in image metadata. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Do not put secrets in ENV.
security: Prefer runtime configuration for values that change per environment.

dockerfile.name: ARG
dockerfile.summary: Defines a build-time variable. Values can be passed with --build-arg and may appear in image history.
dockerfile.description: Defines a build-time variable. Values can be passed with --build-arg and may appear in image history. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: ARG is not suitable for secrets; use BuildKit secrets.
security: ARG before FROM is only available in FROM and must be redeclared in the stage.

dockerfile.name: EXPOSE
dockerfile.summary: Documents the port the container listens on. It does not publish the port.
dockerfile.description: Documents the port the container listens on. It does not publish the port. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Publish with -p or Compose ports; EXPOSE alone is not reachable.
security: Use the actual listen port, not a host port.

dockerfile.name: USER
dockerfile.summary: Sets the user (and optionally group) for subsequent instructions and the runtime.
dockerfile.description: Sets the user (and optionally group) for subsequent instructions and the runtime. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Create the user in the image or use an existing one.
security: Numeric UIDs are more portable across environments.

dockerfile.name: VOLUME
dockerfile.summary: Declares a mount point for external storage. Creates an anonymous volume at runtime if no mount is provided.
dockerfile.description: Declares a mount point for external storage. Creates an anonymous volume at runtime if no mount is provided. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: VOLUME does not make data persistent by itself; mount a named volume.
security: Declaring a VOLUME can complicate later writes in the Dockerfile.

dockerfile.name: HEALTHCHECK
dockerfile.summary: Defines a command that checks container health. Exit 0 is healthy; non-zero is unhealthy.
dockerfile.description: Defines a command that checks container health. Exit 0 is healthy; non-zero is unhealthy. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Use CMD-SHELL for shell syntax, CMD exec form otherwise.
security: Set start-period for slow starters.

dockerfile.name: LABEL
dockerfile.summary: Adds metadata to the image as key-value pairs. Useful for OCI provenance and ownership.
dockerfile.description: Adds metadata to the image as key-value pairs. Useful for OCI provenance and ownership. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Use OCI-standard keys where applicable.
security: Labels are visible in inspect and registries.

dockerfile.name: SHELL
dockerfile.summary: Changes the default shell used by shell-form RUN, CMD and ENTRYPOINT.
dockerfile.description: Changes the default shell used by shell-form RUN, CMD and ENTRYPOINT. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Useful on Windows or when bash features are required.
security: Exec-form instructions bypass the shell.

dockerfile.name: STOPSIGNAL
dockerfile.summary: Sets the signal sent to the container when stopping. Default is SIGTERM.
dockerfile.description: Sets the signal sent to the container when stopping. Default is SIGTERM. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: The application must handle the signal gracefully.
security: Compose has a separate stop_grace_period.

dockerfile.name: ONBUILD
dockerfile.summary: Registers a trigger instruction to run later when the image is used as a base. Avoid in most images.
dockerfile.description: Registers a trigger instruction to run later when the image is used as a base. Avoid in most images. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: ONBUILD makes child builds surprising and hard to debug.
security: Prefer explicit instructions in the child Dockerfile.

dockerfile.name: .dockerignore
dockerfile.summary: Excludes files from the build context. Not a Dockerfile instruction, but critical for cache and context size.
dockerfile.syntax: One pattern per line, with ! for exceptions
dockerfile.description: Excludes files from the build context. Not a Dockerfile instruction, but critical for cache and context size. This is a Dockerfile instruction, not a Docker CLI command.
mistakes: Exclude node_modules and VCS metadata.
security: Negated patterns can re-include files; test with the build output.

properties.name: services
properties.summary: Top-level map of services. Each key is a service name and each value defines a container.
properties.description: Top-level map of services. Each key is a service name and each value defines a container. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Minimal stack
examples.explain: The top-level services map is required in every Compose file. Each key becomes a service name and a DNS name on the project network.

examples.title: Project name plus services
examples.command:
name: acme

services:
  api:
    build: .
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
examples.explain: name sets the Compose project name, which prefixes containers, networks and volumes. It keeps project resources identifiable in a busy engine.

mistakes: services must be a map, not a list. A YAML list fails schema validation before any container starts.
Do not add a top-level version field. It is obsolete in Compose v2 and produces a warning.

properties.name: image
properties.summary: Image reference used to create the service container. Can be combined with build to tag the built image.
properties.description: Image reference used to create the service container. Can be combined with build to tag the built image. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Pinned tag
examples.explain: A full reference includes the registry, repository and tag. Pinning the version makes a deployment reproducible.

examples.title: Build and tag together
examples.explain: When build is present, image names the tag applied to the built result. It also lets other services reference the same image.

mistakes: Using latest in production makes rollbacks ambiguous; two deploys can run different code under the same tag.
A bare name is pulled from Docker Hub by default. Specify the registry when the image does not live there.
security: Pull from registries you trust and verify digests when supply-chain integrity matters.

properties.name: build
properties.summary: Build configuration: context, dockerfile, target, args, cache_from, cache_to, platforms, secrets.
properties.description: Build configuration: context, dockerfile, target, args, cache_from, cache_to, platforms, secrets. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
build:
  context: <path|url>
  dockerfile: <file>
  target: <stage>
  args: <map>
  platforms: <list>
  cache_from: <list>
  cache_to: <list>
  secrets: <list>

examples.title: Multi-stage target
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
      target: runtime
examples.explain: target stops the build at a named stage, so development stages never reach the runtime image.

examples.title: Build arguments
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      args:
        NODE_VERSION: "20"
examples.explain: Build args feed ARG values into the Dockerfile. They are configuration, not secrets.

mistakes: A relative context is resolved from the Compose file location, not from the shell working directory.
Build args are recorded in image history and metadata; never pass credentials through them.
security: Use BuildKit secrets (build.secrets) instead of build args for tokens, keys and passwords.

properties.name: ports
properties.summary: Publishes container ports to the host. Short syntax HOST:CONTAINER; long syntax supports protocol, mode and host_ip.
properties.description: Publishes container ports to the host. Short syntax HOST:CONTAINER; long syntax supports protocol, mode and host_ip. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
ports:
  - "[HOST_IP:]<HOST_PORT>:<CONTAINER_PORT>[/<protocol>]"
  - target: <port>
    published: "<port>"
    protocol: tcp
    mode: host
    host_ip: <ip>

examples.title: Short syntax
examples.explain: The left side is the host port and the right side is the container port. Traffic to host 8080 reaches port 80 in the container.

examples.title: Long syntax with host binding
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    ports:
      - target: 3000
        published: "3000"
        host_ip: 127.0.0.1
        protocol: tcp
examples.explain: The long form makes the host interface explicit. Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps the port off external interfaces.

mistakes: Publishing to 0.0.0.0 exposes the port on every interface, including networks you did not intend.
Reversing host and container ports produces a service that is reachable on the wrong port, or not at all.
security: Publish only ports that must be reachable from outside the host. Keep internal service ports on the project network.

properties.name: expose
properties.summary: Documents ports used internally. Does not publish them to the host.
properties.description: Documents ports used internally. Does not publish them to the host. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Document an internal port
examples.explain: expose records the port the service listens on for other services on the same network. It never publishes a host port.

mistakes: expose does not make a port reachable from the host. Use ports for that.
Exposing a port does not make the application listen on it; the process configuration must match.

properties.name: environment
properties.summary: Map or list of environment variables for the container. Values are visible in inspect; not for secrets.
properties.description: Map or list of environment variables for the container. Values are visible in inspect; not for secrets. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
environment:
  KEY: value
  OTHER: ""
# or
environment:
  - KEY=value

examples.title: Map form
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      LOG_LEVEL: info
examples.explain: The map form is the clearest for a fixed set of values. YAML scalars are converted to strings.

examples.title: Pass a value from the shell
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL}"
examples.explain: Compose interpolates ${...} from the shell or .env before the container starts. The value still appears in inspect.

mistakes: An empty value still defines the variable; it does not unset it.
YAML converts unquoted yes or no to a boolean before Compose sees it. Quote values that must stay text.
security: Environment variables are visible in docker inspect and docker compose config. Use secrets for credentials.

properties.name: env_file
properties.summary: Loads environment variables from one or more files. Can be optional.
properties.description: Loads environment variables from one or more files. Can be optional. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
env_file: <path>
# or
env_file:
  - path: <path>
    required: true

examples.title: Single file
examples.explain: The file is read from the Compose file directory. Each non-comment line becomes an environment variable in the container.

examples.title: Optional file
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    env_file:
      - path: .env.optional
        required: false
examples.explain: required: false lets a local override file be absent without failing the whole project.

mistakes: A path is resolved relative to the Compose file, not the shell. A working directory override changes what you expect.
Values in the environment section take precedence over env_file entries for the same key.
security: Never commit an env file containing live credentials. Add .env files to .gitignore.

properties.name: depends_on
properties.summary: Controls startup order. With condition: service_healthy it waits for a health check; it does not restart dependents later.
properties.description: Controls startup order. With condition: service_healthy it waits for a health check; it does not restart dependents later. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
depends_on:
  - <service>
# or
depends_on:
  <service>:
    condition: service_started|service_healthy|service_completed_successfully
    restart: true

examples.title: Start order only
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    depends_on:
      - db
examples.explain: The short form waits until db has started, not until its process is ready to accept connections.

examples.title: Wait for a healthy dependency
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
examples.explain: The long form waits for the dependency health check to pass. db must define a healthcheck.

mistakes: depends_on does not wait for an application to be ready unless condition: service_healthy is used.
It does not restart dependents if the dependency dies later. The application still needs retries.

properties.name: healthcheck
properties.summary: Defines a health probe with test, interval, timeout, retries, start_period. Enables service_healthy dependencies and --wait.
properties.description: Defines a health probe with test, interval, timeout, retries, start_period. Enables service_healthy dependencies and --wait. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
healthcheck:
  test: ["CMD", "<command>", "<arg>"]
  interval: 30s
  timeout: 5s
  retries: 3
  start_period: 10s
  start_interval: 5s
  disable: false

examples.title: HTTP probe
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-qO-", "http://localhost:3000/health"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
examples.explain: The probe runs inside the container. start_period gives a slow starter time before failures count.

examples.title: Shell probe
examples.command:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 10s
      retries: 5
examples.explain: CMD-SHELL runs the string through the container shell, which is needed for pipes and redirection.

mistakes: curl is missing from many minimal images. Use a tool that exists in the image or build one in.
A health check that always exits 0 hides failures. Probe the dependency the service actually needs.
security: Health commands run inside the container with the service user. Do not put credentials in the test string.

properties.name: volumes
properties.summary: Mounts named volumes, bind mounts or tmpfs. Named volumes must be declared at the top level to be managed as project resources.
properties.description: Mounts named volumes, bind mounts or tmpfs. Named volumes must be declared at the top level to be managed as project resources. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
volumes:
  - <volume-name>:<container-path>[:ro]
  - type: volume|bind|tmpfs
    source: <name|path>
    target: <path>
    read_only: true

# top level
volumes:
  <volume-name>: {}

examples.title: Named volume
examples.command:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  db-data: {}
examples.explain: A named volume is managed by Docker, survives container removal and is declared once at the top level.

examples.title: Read-only bind mount
examples.explain: A path on the left is a bind mount from the host. :ro makes the mount read-only inside the container.

mistakes: A short-syntax source without a slash is a named volume, not a host path. ./site and site mean different things.
A named volume used by a service but missing from top-level volumes is created implicitly and is harder to manage.
security: Never mount /var/run/docker.sock into an application container; it grants control of the engine.
Bind mounts expose host files and permissions. Prefer named volumes for application data.

properties.name: networks
properties.summary: Attaches a service to one or more networks by name. Networks can be declared at the top level with driver and options.
properties.description: Attaches a service to one or more networks by name. Networks can be declared at the top level with driver and options. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
services:
  <service>:
    networks:
      - <network>

networks:
  <network>:
    driver: bridge|overlay
    internal: true

examples.title: Two-service private network
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    networks:
      - backend
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    networks:
      - backend

networks:
  backend: {}
examples.explain: Only services on backend can resolve and reach each other. The network is prefixed with the project name.

examples.title: Internal network
examples.explain: internal: true removes the gateway, so services cannot reach the outside world through it.

mistakes: A service can only reach a service on a shared network. The default network is not shared with another project.
Network names are prefixed by the project unless name is set explicitly.
security: Use internal networks for databases and other services that should never reach the internet.

properties.name: secrets
properties.summary: Mounts sensitive values from files or environment into /run/secrets by default. Keeps secrets out of images and env.
properties.description: Mounts sensitive values from files or environment into /run/secrets by default. Keeps secrets out of images and env. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
services:
  <service>:
    secrets:
      - <secret>
      - source: <secret>
        target: <filename>
        mode: 0400

secrets:
  <secret>:
    file: <path>
# or
    environment: <ENV_VAR>

examples.title: Mount a secret file
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    secrets:
      - db_password

secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt
examples.explain: The secret appears as /run/secrets/db_password inside the container. It is not an environment variable.

examples.title: Read a secret from the environment
examples.explain: The value comes from the host environment at deploy time and is mounted as a file, not exported into the container environment.

mistakes: The application must read the secret from /run/secrets; it will not appear in env.
Changing a secret file requires recreating the service for the new content to be mounted.
security: Compose secrets are files, not a vault. Protect the source file and restrict its mode.
Do not bake secrets into images or commit them to the repository.

properties.name: configs
properties.summary: Mounts non-secret configuration files. Similar lifecycle to secrets but semantically public.
properties.description: Mounts non-secret configuration files. Similar lifecycle to secrets but semantically public. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
services:
  <service>:
    configs:
      - <config>
      - source: <config>
        target: <path>

configs:
  <config>:
    file: <path>

examples.title: Mount configuration
examples.command:
services:
  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    configs:
      - source: nginx_conf
        target: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf

configs:
  nginx_conf:
    file: ./nginx/default.conf
examples.explain: Configs use the same mount mechanism as secrets but are suitable for non-sensitive content.

mistakes: Configs are read-only inside the container; the application must not try to rewrite them.
A config change requires recreating the service just like a secret change.
security: Do not use configs for passwords or keys. Use secrets instead.

properties.name: profiles
properties.summary: Opt-in service groups. A service with profiles does not start unless the profile is enabled.
properties.description: Opt-in service groups. A service with profiles does not start unless the profile is enabled. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
services:
  <service>:
    profiles:
      - <profile>
# enable with: docker compose --profile <profile> up

examples.title: Opt-in debug tools
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
  adminer:
    image: adminer:4
    profiles:
      - tools
examples.explain: docker compose up starts only api. docker compose --profile tools up adds adminer.

mistakes: A service with profiles does not start by default, even if another service depends on it.
An enabled profile does not start services from other profiles. Each profile must be requested.
security: Put administrative and debugging services behind a profile so they are not exposed by a normal start.

properties.name: restart
properties.summary: Restart policy: no, on-failure[:max], always, unless-stopped.
properties.description: Restart policy: no, on-failure[:max], always, unless-stopped. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Restart on failure
examples.command:
services:
  worker:
    image: acme/worker:1.4.2
    restart: on-failure:5
examples.explain: The container restarts up to five times after a non-zero exit. A clean exit stops the loop.

examples.title: Survive daemon restarts
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    restart: unless-stopped
examples.explain: unless-stopped restarts after daemon restarts but respects an explicit docker stop.

mistakes: restart: always restarts even after a clean exit, which can hide a completed one-shot job.
A restart loop is a symptom. Fix the failing process instead of increasing the retry count.

properties.name: deploy
properties.summary: Deployment-related settings, including resources.limits and replicas (Compose supports limits on a single host; replicas and placement are orchestrator features).
properties.description: Deployment-related settings, including resources.limits and replicas (Compose supports limits on a single host; replicas and placement are orchestrator features). This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
deploy:
  replicas: <n>
  resources:
    limits:
      cpus: "<cores>"
      memory: <size>
    reservations:
      cpus: "<cores>"
      memory: <size>

examples.title: Resource limits
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 256M
examples.explain: Limits cap the container. Docker Compose applies these on a single host for local deployments.

examples.title: Replicas on a single host
examples.command:
services:
  worker:
    image: acme/worker:1.4.2
    deploy:
      replicas: 3
examples.explain: Replica count is an orchestration feature. Compose honors it when scaling the project, not as a scheduler.

mistakes: Replicas and placement are scheduling features; a one-shot docker compose up is not a Swarm scheduler.
Memory values need a unit (256M). A bare number is parsed as bytes and surprises you.
security: Limits protect the host from a runaway container, but they are not a security boundary.

properties.name: logging
properties.summary: Logging driver and options for the service, such as max-size and max-file for json-file.
properties.description: Logging driver and options for the service, such as max-size and max-file for json-file. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.
properties.syntax:
logging:
  driver: json-file|local|syslog|journald|none
  options:
    max-size: "10m"
    max-file: "3"

examples.title: Bounded json-file logs
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    logging:
      driver: json-file
      options:
        max-size: "10m"
        max-file: "3"
examples.explain: Rotation keeps log files bounded. Without it, json-file logs grow until the disk fills.

mistakes: The default json-file driver has no size limit. Long-running services eventually fill the disk.
A driver must be available on the host; an unknown driver fails container creation.
security: Logs can contain personal data and tokens. Set retention deliberately and restrict access to the log files.

properties.name: command
properties.summary: Overrides the image CMD.
properties.description: Overrides the image CMD. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Exec form
examples.explain: The list form runs without a shell, so signals reach the process directly.

examples.title: Override a long-running command
examples.explain: command replaces the image CMD. It does not touch ENTRYPOINT.

mistakes: A string is run through /bin/sh -c, which changes signal handling and quoting.
command does not replace ENTRYPOINT. If the entrypoint expects arguments, keep them compatible.

properties.name: entrypoint
properties.summary: Overrides the image ENTRYPOINT.
properties.description: Overrides the image ENTRYPOINT. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Exec form entrypoint
examples.explain: entrypoint replaces the image ENTRYPOINT and receives command arguments after it.

mistakes: Clearing an entrypoint with [] is sometimes needed for shell images, but can break the image contract.
A shell-form entrypoint swallows signals. Prefer the exec form.

properties.name: user
properties.summary: Sets the user for the container process.
properties.description: Sets the user for the container process. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Numeric user
examples.explain: Numeric IDs work even when /etc/passwd has no matching name. The image must allow that user to write its paths.

mistakes: A user that does not exist in /etc/passwd may still run by numeric UID, but tools that resolve names fail.
Mounts and application directories must be writable by the chosen UID or the process exits immediately.
security: Run as non-root where possible. Check file ownership before switching the user.

properties.name: working_dir
properties.summary: Sets the working directory inside the container.
properties.description: Sets the working directory inside the container. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Set the process directory
examples.explain: The container process starts in this directory. Relative paths in command resolve from here.

mistakes: The directory must exist in the image; Compose does not create it for you.
A relative path is resolved inside the container, not on the host.

properties.name: read_only
properties.summary: Mounts the root filesystem read-only. Combine with tmpfs or volumes for writable paths.
properties.description: Mounts the root filesystem read-only. Combine with tmpfs or volumes for writable paths. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Read-only root with writable tmp
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
    volumes:
      - api-cache:/var/cache/app

volumes:
  api-cache: {}
examples.explain: The root filesystem cannot be modified, while /tmp and the named volume stay writable.

mistakes: Applications that write to the root filesystem fail at start. Audit writable paths first.
read_only does not make mounted volumes read-only. Add :ro or read_only: true per mount.
security: A read-only root filesystem limits what an attacker can persist inside the container.

properties.name: cap_drop
properties.summary: Drops Linux capabilities. Use ["ALL"] then add only what is required.
properties.description: Drops Linux capabilities. Use ["ALL"] then add only what is required. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Drop everything
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
examples.explain: Start from no capabilities and add back only what the process demonstrably needs.

mistakes: Dropping ALL without testing can break a service that relied on a default capability such as CHOWN.
Adding capabilities back without a reason defeats the purpose of dropping them.
security: Never add SYS_ADMIN or NET_ADMIN unless the workload is genuinely privileged and isolated.

properties.name: security_opt
properties.summary: Security options such as no-new-privileges and seccomp/apparmor profiles.
properties.description: Security options such as no-new-privileges and seccomp/apparmor profiles. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: No privilege escalation
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
examples.explain: The process cannot gain privileges through setuid binaries or file capabilities.

mistakes: Referencing a seccomp profile that does not exist on the host prevents the container from starting.
Disabling seccomp or AppArmor removes a real boundary; do not do it to silence a permission error.
security: Keep the default seccomp profile. Prefer narrowing it rather than disabling it.

properties.name: tmpfs
properties.summary: Mounts an in-memory filesystem. Useful for writable temporary paths with read_only.
properties.description: Mounts an in-memory filesystem. Useful for writable temporary paths with read_only. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Bounded tmpfs
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:size=64m,mode=1777
examples.explain: In-memory storage is ideal for ephemeral files on a read-only root. The size cap prevents memory exhaustion.

mistakes: tmpfs contents are lost when the container stops and count against memory.
An uncapped tmpfs can consume the host memory allocated to the container.
security: Cap tmpfs size so a compromised process cannot exhaust memory through temporary files.

properties.name: stop_grace_period
properties.summary: How long to wait after SIGTERM before SIGKILL when stopping the container.
properties.description: How long to wait after SIGTERM before SIGKILL when stopping the container. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Allow a slow shutdown
examples.explain: Docker sends SIGTERM, waits the grace period, then sends SIGKILL. Give the application time to drain.

mistakes: A grace period shorter than the application drain time turns a graceful shutdown into SIGKILL.
The application must handle SIGTERM. A process that ignores it always reaches SIGKILL.

properties.name: init
properties.summary: Runs a small init process as PID 1 to reap zombies and forward signals.
properties.description: Runs a small init process as PID 1 to reap zombies and forward signals. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Enable the init process
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    init: true
examples.explain: A tiny init runs as PID 1, reaps orphaned processes and forwards signals to the application.

mistakes: init is not a substitute for handling signals in the application.
Some images already include an init or an entrypoint that execs the process; adding another can be redundant.

properties.name: extra_hosts
properties.summary: Adds host-to-IP mappings to /etc/hosts.
properties.description: Adds host-to-IP mappings to /etc/hosts. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Map a host name
examples.explain: host-gateway resolves to the host address on Linux. It lets a container reach a service running on the host.

mistakes: Hard-coding an IP breaks when the host network changes. Prefer host-gateway where supported.
extra_hosts changes name resolution only; it does not open a firewall path.
security: Reaching the host from a container widens the attack surface. Use it deliberately.

properties.name: dns
properties.summary: Custom DNS servers for the service.
properties.description: Custom DNS servers for the service. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Custom resolver
examples.explain: The container uses these resolvers instead of the host configuration for external names.

mistakes: Custom DNS replaces the embedded Docker DNS for external lookups; service discovery on the project network still works.
A resolver that is not reachable from the container breaks name resolution entirely.
security: DNS traffic can leak metadata. Use resolvers you trust.

properties.name: ulimits
properties.summary: Sets ulimit values such as nofile.
properties.description: Sets ulimit values such as nofile. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Raise open-file limits
examples.command:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    ulimits:
      nofile:
        soft: 65536
        hard: 65536
examples.explain: The soft limit is the effective value; the hard limit caps what the process can raise.

mistakes: A hard limit above the host limit fails at container start.
Raising nofile without checking application connection pools can exhaust other resources.

properties.name: platform
properties.summary: Forces a specific platform for the service image.
properties.description: Forces a specific platform for the service image. This is a Compose YAML property, not a CLI flag.

examples.title: Force an architecture
examples.command:
services:
  legacy:
    image: acme/legacy:1.0
    platform: linux/amd64
examples.explain: Useful when only a specific architecture is published. On an ARM host the image runs under emulation and is slower.

mistakes: Emulated platforms are slower and may behave differently for native dependencies.
The image must exist for the requested platform, or the pull fails.
security: Emulation layers widen the supply chain. Pin the platform only when the image requires it.
